name: Colossians
author: The letter opens in the name of Paul, a Jewish teacher and former persecutor of Christians who became a travelling missionary planting churches across the Roman world, with his young co-worker Timothy. Paul writes as a prisoner, traditionally in Rome around AD 60–62, though some suggest an earlier imprisonment in Ephesus. Many scholars think a close follower wrote it in Paul's name after his death, pointing to differences in style and emphasis; others see no reason to doubt Paul himself.
audience: It was written to a small church in Colossae, a town in the Lycus River valley in what is now western Turkey, near the larger cities of Laodicea and Hierapolis. Paul had never visited them, and most believers there seem to have been Gentiles (non-Jews) who had only recently turned to Christ from local religions.
era: The Roman Empire ruled the region, with Nero as emperor from AD 54 to 68. Colossae had once been a busy wool-trading town but was being overshadowed by nearby Laodicea, and the valley was home to a mix of Greek, local Phrygian and Jewish communities. A powerful earthquake struck the area around AD 60. Christians were still a tiny, little-understood group meeting in homes.

notes.1:3: Epaphras, a local man from Colossae, had first brought the Christian message there and had come to Paul with news of the church.
notes.1:15: Many scholars think this section may be an early Christian hymn or poem, possibly already sung in worship, which the writer included here.
notes.1:24: Paul writes from prison and mentions believers in nearby Laodicea too, churches he had never visited in person.
notes.2:6: This section answers teachers in Colossae promoting a religious philosophy built on human traditions; exactly who they were and what they taught is still debated.
notes.2:16: Some were pressing the church about food rules, festivals, new moons, Sabbath days and worship of angels, likely a blend of Jewish practices and local spiritual ideas.
notes.3:18: This follows the pattern of 'household rules' common in Greek and Roman moral writing, addressing husbands, wives, children, fathers, slaves and masters in one home.
notes.4:7: Tychicus carried the letter with Onesimus, the enslaved man also named in Paul's letter to Philemon. Near the end, the letter also mentions a letter to Laodicea; most think it has been lost, though some suggest it may be another surviving letter such as Ephesians.
